questions.question: Describe why and how the Castle of Good Hope was built.
questions.expected_answer: In 1652, the Dutch East India Company set up a station at the Cape, led by Jan van Riebeeck, to supply its ships with fresh food and water, first building a fort of clay and wood. From 1666 to 1679, it built the stone Castle, a pentagon with five bastions so soldiers could fire along the walls, using stone from around Table Mountain and Robben Island and the labour of soldiers, sailors and enslaved people.

questions.question: Explain how the Castle meant different things to different people.
questions.expected_answer: For the Dutch East India Company, it was the centre of power where the governor ruled and laws were read. For the Khoikhoi, it symbolised the loss of their land and grazing, and conflict, though some worked or traded there. For enslaved people, it was a place of forced labour and harsh punishment. Later, it was the headquarters of the British army and then used by the South African army.

questions.question: What does the Castle teach us about heritage and changing identities?
questions.expected_answer: Identities changed at the Cape as Khoikhoi, Europeans and enslaved people from Africa and Asia lived together, forming new communities, cultures and the Afrikaans language. The Castle's identity changed too: once a symbol of colonial power, it is now a museum open to all that tells the stories of the Khoikhoi and enslaved people as well. This shows that heritage is not fixed and can include voices that were left out.
